title: Ang 1360–1364: Gatha, Funhe, Chaubole
hook: short, dense poems of Guru Arjan
tomorrow: a saint calls himself the worst of all, and the Lord's dog. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, on ang 1353, the old style: Guru Nanak in the pandits' own accent, saying learning without the One is empty. Now the poems shrink.

A text that says only 'outside' can hold a whole evening: I made it, I'm here, come down. Short can be full. A few pages after the old style, on ang 1361, Guru Arjan writes small verses called Funhe, and each one ends on the same word: harihaan, a call to the Lord. Before them comes the Gatha; after them, the Chaubole. Three tiny forms on a handful of pages. What does short do that long can't?
screen: `ONE WORD: OUTSIDE.` → `EACH VERSE ENDS: HARIHAAN.` → `WHAT CAN SHORT DO?`

segments.voice: Start with the Funhe. Each verse paints one picture, of longing for the Beloved, of the world's pull, of the company of the holy, and then the last word turns the picture into a call: harihaan. No explanation follows. The verse trusts the picture. The Gatha, before them, works the same way in another old style: the body that passes, the Name that lasts, said once and left. Then the Chaubole. These verses are addressed to people by name, as if handed to them, and one of them, in paraphrase, says: if this love could be bought with money, the rich would never go without it. That's the whole verse's argument, in a single picture. Love isn't for sale, and the poem doesn't spend a word more proving it. So what does short do? It makes you finish the thought. A long hymn walks you all the way. A dense verse hands you the picture and stops, and the stopping is part of the teaching, because the listener has to carry the rest. Guru Arjan wrote long hymns too. Here he shows the other skill: knowing exactly where to stop.
screen: `FUNHE: A PICTURE, THEN HARIHAAN.` · `GATHA: SAID ONCE AND LEFT.` · `CHAUBOLE: LOVE ISN'T FOR SALE.` · `THE STOP IS PART OF IT.` · then, large: `DENSE AND SHORT.`

segments.voice: Write one line by hand about something that matters to you this week. Cross out every word that isn't carrying weight, until only the picture is left. Then let the sit hold that last version.
Ang 1360. Where the Gatha begins, then the Funhe and the Chaubole: Guru Arjan's smallest forms, a picture and a stop.
Your line: dense and short. One picture, then stop, and let the listener carry the rest. Day done.

howItsDone: The Gatha, Funhe and Chaubole are read in the closing pages of the Granth; in kirtan the Funhe are sometimes sung with harihaan drawn out at the end of each verse.

fork.setup: your cousin's wedding speech is ten minutes of thank-yous, and the room is drifting. she asks you to help. what do the Funhe suggest?
options: keep one true picture of the couple, then stop and let it land.
keep every name; leaving anyone out is rude, so length is kinder.
cut it to 'congrats, love you both,' and sit right back down.
fork.reveal: the Funhe aren't bare; they're full. one picture, a word that turns it toward the One, and a stop. short for its own sake misses it; dense is the point.
